books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

primary_sources: Andrew Jackson, letter to Henry Lee, October 7, 1825

stimulus.text: “Mr. Adams is the Constitutional President and as such I would myself be the last man in the Commonwealth to oppose him upon any other ground than that of principle. How he reached the office is an enquiry for the succeeding canvass, when the principles of the Constitution, apart from his ministerial acts, or at least without necessary opposition to them, will sanction the investigation.” — Andrew Jackson, letter to Henry Lee, October 7, 1825.
stimulus.source_note: Andrew Jackson, letter to Henry Lee, October 7, 1825. Verbatim quotation; wording verified against the Library of Congress citation of the letter. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The election Jackson describes was settled by a deal in the House of Representatives. Which later election was settled in the most similar way?

options.text: The election of 1828, when Jackson defeated Adams
options.misconception: Jackson won 1828 outright at the polls; no House deal settled it.

options.text: The election of 1860, when Lincoln defeated Douglas and the South seceded
options.misconception: Lincoln won the Electoral College outright, and the result led to secession, not a bargain.

options.text: The election of 1896, when McKinley defeated Bryan
options.misconception: McKinley won outright; Populists cried foul, but no deal handed him the presidency.

options.text: The election of 1876, when Hayes became president after a disputed count

rationales.A: Jackson won 1828 outright, so no deal was needed to settle it.
rationales.B: Lincoln won the Electoral College outright in 1860; the crisis was secession, not a bargain.
rationales.C: McKinley won outright in 1896; there was no deal trading the presidency.
rationales.D: Like 1824, the election of 1876 was settled by a backroom bargain in Congress: Hayes took the presidency and Reconstruction ended.
rationales.general:
1. Name the 1824 pattern. No candidate won an electoral majority, the House chose Adams, and Clay took the secretaryship.
2. Test each later election. In 1828, 1860, and 1896 the winner took the Electoral College outright, so no deal was needed.
3. Match the pattern. In 1876 the count was disputed and a congressional bargain made Hayes president.
Background: The 1876 bargain, the Compromise of 1877, traded the presidency for the end of Reconstruction in the South.
Remember: when no one wins cleanly, look for who cuts the deal.
